paragraphs.text: Autosomal recessive juvenile Parkinson disease (AR-JP) is a levodopa-responsive parkinsonism. Its pathologic hallmark is a highly selective degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the zona compacta of the substantia nigra (Matsumine et al., 1997). Ishikawa and Tsuji (1996) considered AR-JP a distinct clinical entity within juvenile parkinsonism, because their patients had similar clinical findings that differed from those of other types of parkinsonism. Matsumine et al. (1998) described the 6q-linked disorder as having a benign clinical course and relatively selective degeneration of nigral dopaminergic neurons without Lewy body formation.

paragraphs.text: Takahashi et al. (1994) described a family in which 4 of 5 sibs, born to first-cousin parents, developed parkinsonism at similarly early ages. The parkinsonism improved after sleep. One affected sib, a 67-year-old woman, came to autopsy. Pathologic changes were confined to the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNPC) and the locus ceruleus. The medial and ventrolateral SNPC showed obvious neuronal loss and gliosis. Elsewhere in the SNPC and in the locus ceruleus, neurons were fewer and most had low melanin content, without detectable gliosis or extraneuronal free melanin. There were no Lewy bodies, and the authors concluded that the overall pathology differed from that of Lewy body Parkinson disease.

paragraphs.text: Sasaki et al. (2004) reported autopsy findings in a patient with AR-JP. Brain lesions were limited to dopaminergic neuron systems such as the substantia nigra and locus ceruleus. Melanin-containing neurons in the SNPC were moderately to severely depleted, with gliosis. Neurons in the locus ceruleus were mildly decreased, and melanin pigment was seen outside neurons. There were no Lewy bodies in the neuropil of the SNPC or locus ceruleus. Occasional doughnut-shaped or round basophilic inclusion bodies in the neuropil of the pedunculopontine nucleus stained for alpha-synuclein and ubiquitin. The authors concluded that different parkin gene abnormalities may cause differences in the degree and distribution of neuronal degeneration, including whether Lewy bodies are present. paragraphs.text: Mortiboys et al. (2008) studied fibroblasts from 5 parkin-mutant patients. Mitochondrial membrane potential was reduced by about 30% in glucose medium and 70% in galactose medium. Complex I activity was reduced by about 42%, with normal complex III and IV activity, and complex I-linked (but not complex II-linked) ATP production was reduced. Cellular ATP levels were reduced by 58%, but cell viability and growth were unaffected. Mitochondrial branching was increased, and this correlated with lower complex I-linked ATP production and complex I activity, suggesting that the functional and morphologic effects of parkin deficiency on mitochondria are related. FRAP assays showed reduced functional connectivity of the mitochondrial matrix, which worsened with rotenone. Rotenone shortened mitochondria in parkin-mutant but not control cells. Knockdown of parkin by 80% with siRNA in control fibroblasts reduced mitochondrial membrane potential and cellular ATP and increased mitochondrial branching by 70%, indicating that parkin deficiency is sufficient to explain the defects in patient cells. In contrast, 50% knockdown, mimicking haploinsufficiency, had no effect. The authors considered this consistent with true recessive inheritance and not supportive of heterozygosity as a PD risk factor.
